query: High-entropy alloys contain five or more elements at 5–35 at% each, generally with comparable atomic radii. Refractory and nickel-based high-entropy alloys have demonstrated elevated-temperature mechanical properties comparable to titanium- and nickel-based alloys used in extreme environments because of their heat resistance and specific strength. However, prior investigations have mainly treated titanium and nickel as additions, leaving alloys in which both are primary constituents unexplored. Subject to the stated compositional definition, what single testable intervention hypothesis could improve the elevated-temperature mechanical properties of a titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy relative to the same material without the intervention? Specify the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted relative outcome, composition and operating boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment with explicit results that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled post-deposition heat treatment that promotes a fine, thermally stable precipitation of Ti2Ni phase within a titanium‐ and nickel‐primary high-entropy alloy will improve its elevated-temperature mechanical properties relative to an untreated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents (with additional elements ensuring 5–35 at% each) produced via additive manufacturing (e.g., direct energy deposition) with a fine as-deposited microstructure containing phases such as Ti2Ni in small amounts.
generation.intervention: Apply a post-deposition annealing cycle (for example, holding at 800°C for a controlled period, such as 1–2 hours) that is below the alloy’s incipient melting point to allow controlled precipitation.
generation.conditions: Annealing temperature in the range of approximately 750–850°C for 1–2 hours under an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation, while maintaining the compositional uniformity (each element at 5–35 at%) and avoiding coarsening beyond the beneficial fine scale.
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of a fine, dispersed Ti2Ni precipitate phase within the matrix.
generation.mechanism: The controlled heat treatment facilitates the formation of finely dispersed Ti2Ni precipitates that act as obstacles to dislocation motion and grain-boundary sliding, thereby enhancing creep resistance and yield strength at elevated temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Elevated-temperature mechanical properties (e.g., yield strength and creep strength) will be improved in the post-annealed alloy relative to the as-deposited material, owing to enhanced precipitation strengthening and grain stabilization; the improvement is expected to be measurable, although the exact magnitude is uncertain.
generation.baseline: The same titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy in its as-deposited state (without any post-deposition heat treatment).
generation.boundary: The intervention applies only when the alloy composition adheres to the high-entropy alloy definition (5–35 at% per element), when the annealing temperature remains below the incipient melting temperature to prevent unwanted grain growth or degradation, and when processing is performed in an inert atmosphere.
generation.uncertainty: The precise extent of the mechanical property improvements (e.g., percent increase in yield and creep strength) is not well established and may depend on exact heat treatment parameters and initial microstructural condition.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples of the titanium- and nickel-primary high-entropy alloy using the same additive manufacturing process. Subject one set to the controlled post-deposition annealing (750–850°C for 1–2 hours) under an inert atmosphere, while keeping the other set as-deposited. Using identical elevated-temperature testing conditions (e.g., tensile tests and creep tests at temperatures relevant to application), compare the mechanical properties of the two sets.
measurements: Creep strength and strain rate under constant load
Microstructural characterization using SEM, EBSD, and XRD to quantify the presence, size, and distribution of Ti2Ni precipitates
Grain size distribution before and after heat treatment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in elevated-temperature mechanical properties (such as yield strength and creep resistance) compared to the as-deposited samples, or if the anticipated fine Ti2Ni precipitate phase is absent or coarsened in a manner that does not improve mechanical performance, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) are composed of 5–35 at% of five or more elements, have high configurational entropy, do not form intermetallic compounds, and have a single-phase face-centered cubic structure or body-centered cubic structure. In particular, refractory HEAs (RHEAs), based on refractory materials with excellent mechanical properties at high temperatures, have high strength and hardness at room temperature and excellent mechanical properties at low and high temperatures. In this study, the Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al RHEAs were deposited using direct energy deposition (DED). In the microstructure of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al, the sigma, BCC A2, and Ti2Ni phases appeared to be different from the BCC A2, BCC B2, and Laves phases predicted in the phase diagram. This microstructure was similar to that of the casted Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al and had a constructed fine grain size. It was found that the growth of these microstructures was due to the DED process, which has a fast solidification rate. The fine grain size caused high hardness, and the microhardness of the Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al was measured to be about 900 HV. In this study, a Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al RHEA was deposited using DED. The phase diagram and phase fraction of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al were analyzed for deposition on Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. For the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al, powders of each element were mixed to prepare a mixed Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al powder and deposited on Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 substrates. The microstructure and hardness of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al were measured. In addition, HAZ and thermal shielding analyses were performed on the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. The primary findings of this study are as follows: SEM images and EBSD analysis were used to investigate the microstructure of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al. Phase analysis predicted that the BCC B2 phase was 62.2%, the BCC A2 phase was 21.6%, and C14 Laves phase was 16.2%. However, the σ phase was 64.2%, the BCC A2 phase was 28.2%, and the Ti2Ni phase was 7.6% in the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al.The microstructure of the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al consisted of a phase not predicted by the phase analysis but showed a microstructure similar to that of Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al annealed after casting. In addition, the deposited Ti-Nb-Cr-V-Ni-Al exhibited a fine grain size of 1–35 μm.
